transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
President Trump held a state dinner at the White House last night for Chinese leader
Xi Jinping.
This followed meetings earlier in the day.
Neither man released much detail about their discussions.
NPR's Deepa Shivram says they did talk about AI.
U.S. and Chinese officials had deliberated over information-sharing systems that would
help alert each other over AI incidents that would affect national security.
And that would have been a huge development in AI security globally because there are
not a lot of guardrails that exist for this technology.
But it's unclear how far that proposal on AI will actually go because in his remarks
on Thursday morning, Trump was clear that on AI he wants to "leave it exactly where
it is."
NPR's Deepa Shivram reporting.
President Trump denied TV networks CNN and MSNow access to the state banquet at the White
House last night.
The ban came even after a federal judge had ordered the White House to restore access
to media organizations that Trump ousted last weekend.
Some journalists were able to return during the day, but Trump kept others out of the
banquet.
A Democratic senator is asking the White House for immediate answers about a new television
ad featuring President Trump.
The ad says it is paid for by the U.S. government.
NPR's Tamara Keith reports the White House insists it is a public service announcement.
The ad features President Trump's voice and a splashy montage of images of the president.
Phrases including largest tax cut in history flash on the screen as the song providing
the soundtrack to the 30-second ad repeats the phrase, "Love me."
"America will never be a communist country."
In a letter demanding answers, Democratic senator from New Hampshire Maggie Hassan says
the ad appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against using government funds for propaganda.
A White House spokesperson described the ad as a public service announcement.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
The Senate Health Committee spent about two hours yesterday questioning Dr. Heidi Overton.
NPR's Sydney Lupkin reports she is President Trump's nominee to lead the Food and Drug
Administration.
Others asked Overton about her views on vaccines, the abortion pill mifepristone, food safety,
and whether she'll be able to tell the president when he is wrong.
She was serving as a White House aide until her nomination last month.
She stood near the president in the Oval Office this summer when, without evidence, he called
the MMR vaccine potentially quite lethal.
When the committee members asked about that, she didn't say the president was wrong.
But she did say the vaccine is safe, effective, and the best tool in the fight against the
ongoing measles outbreak.
It is not yet clear whether the senators will vote in favor of confirming her.
Sydney Lupkin, NPR News.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
A lawyer for a Pennsylvania man, wounded when a gunman tried to assassinate President Trump
in 2024, says that man has now died.
A lawyer for James Copenhaver says he was hit in the arm and abdomen during the shooting
at the Pennsylvania campaign rally.
The lawyer did not say if Copenhaver's death was directly related to the shooting.
Another man was killed by the 20-year-old gunman.
A third was wounded.
President Trump's ear was grazed.
The gunman was killed.
Mortgage rates are above 7 percent this week, their highest level, since January 2025.
NPR's Stephen Bisaha says that's driven in large part by the U.S. war against Iran.
The war's been creating a lot of volatility in the bond market, which affects the cost
of borrowing, including for a home.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is at 7.03 percent, according to Freddie Mac.
That's a full percentage point higher than it was before the war started in late February.
Getting a standard loan for a $400,000 home today versus back then means paying hundreds
of dollars more each month.
Other factors are also worrying bond traders, like the Federal Reserve raising interest
rates last week.
A modest move, but some of the Fed's policymakers are signaling more rate hikes could be on
the way.
Stephen Bisaha, NPR News.
Thousands of people turned out in a sports stadium in Pretoria, South Africa yesterday.
They were trying to break the world record for "the biggest cookout."
Organizers say they were aiming for 3,000 people for the big grill.
The Guinness Book of World Records has not yet determined if they, in fact, set the cookout
record.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News.

topics.text: President Trump held state dinner at White House for Chinese leader Xi Jinping with meetings on AI
Trump administration denied CNN and MSNow access to state banquet despite federal judge's media access order
Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan questions White House about Trump ad paid for with government funds
Senate Health Committee questions Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump's FDA nominee, on vaccines and mifepristone
Pennsylvania man James Copenhaver, wounded in 2024 Trump assassination attempt, has died
Mortgage rates rise above 7 percent, highest since January, driven by U.S. war against Iran
South Africa attempts to break world record for largest cookout with thousands in Pretoria stadium
